newsitem.title: CHINA: Speculators position for HK dollar attack - traders.
newsitem.headline: Speculators position for HK dollar attack - traders.

text.p: Hong Kong money market traders said fund managers around the world were preparing to attack the Hong Kong dollar, buying currency forwards aggressively.

"It's the usual case where people want to speculate against the currency and they have to fund themselves first," said one head currency trader at a local bank. "Fund managers around the world will be trying to attack the Hong Kong dollar and they are trying to buy forwards."

Traders said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was intervening heavily as currency forwards reached their highest levels since the 1995 speculative attack against the Hong Kong dollar, which followed the Mexican peso crisis.
Three-month currency fowards reached 350 points while the six-month soared to 550 from Wednesday's levels of 130 and 170 respectively.
The Hong Kong dollar spot rate remained steady at HK$7.7428/38. The unit is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment on market conditions, or confirm its intervention.

"We will closely monitor the situation," said HKMA spokesman Thoman Chan. "I've just come back from the dealing rooms, I know what is happening in the market, I know what traders have said to reporters. The HKMA will monitor the market and we don't comment on money market rumours."
Dealers said funds were buying U.S. dollar foward, anticipating a fall in the Hong Kong dollar.
"It's speculation and the spillover from speculation," said Callum Henderson at MMS International. "Previously banks wouldn't necessarily hedge their short U.S. dollar exposure."

Customers bailing out of Hong Kong dollars are leaving Hong Kong banks short of U.S. dollars short-term. Banks are now going to the market to make sure they are not exposed to the Hong Kong dollar, Henderson said, where previously they would not bother.
Although the HKMA declined to comment, traders said the HKMA was mopping up liquidity in the short end, keeping conditions tight by buying up all the excess Hong Kong currency.
One dealer reported the HKMA selling one-month Hong Kong dollar Exchange Fund bills at 7.71 percent -- far above the one-month market yield of 6.56 percent.
"He (HKMA chief Joseph Yam) hit the market twice. We expect short-dated money will squeeze up dramatically on Friday," the dealer said.
Two initial public offerings were due to be released on Friday, which would tighten liquidity further in Hong Kong's small and tightly-traded money market.
The overnight shot above the key level of seven percent this morning before settling back to 6.75 percent after intervention.
Dealers said they were very nervous that rates would soar sky-high on Friday, forcing them to bail out of positions.
"We will take losses. The mood, in one word, is very frightened," the dealer said.

"(The spot rate) didn't do what (Yam) wanted it to after he intervened on Friday. It still went back to HK$7.75 and this made him crazy and angry. Tomorrow is a good day, he can do anything. He can squeeze rates up to 55 percent if he wants."

But some players said the activity was driven more by "prudent hedging" than speculation. Substantial scepticism about the likelihood of a successful attack against the Hong Kong dollar remained much in evidence as the morning session closed.
The HKMA holds at least US$63 billion in foreign exchange reserves, and has a commitment of support from China, which holds in excess of US$112 billion in foreign exchange.
